classification.illumination_detail: 6500K white LED behind push-thru acrylic letters; amber LED faux-neon flexible tubing in channel letters; E27 medium-base sockets with amber LED lamps as an exposed marquee-bulb border

knowledge.plain_language_summary: Option 1 of three for a tall double-sided projecting blade sign in a theater-marquee idiom, mounted perpendicular to the building on square-tube arms so it reads down the sidewalk both ways. This option stacks the venue name as internally lit push-thru acrylic letters over a painted aluminum body, framed by faux-neon channel letters and an exposed amber-bulb border that animates the edge at night.
knowledge.rationale: A projecting blade is the correct device for a storefront theater on a pedestrian street because it is read along the sidewalk rather than head-on; combining push-thru letters, faux neon, and an exposed-lamp border layers three illumination techniques to get the vintage marquee read while using LED sources for service life.
knowledge.tradeoffs: Stacking push-thru, faux neon, and socketed lamp borders gives the richest, most animated marquee of the three options at the cost of the highest fabrication complexity and the most failure points to service.
knowledge.when_to_use: Pedestrian-facing entertainment venues wanting a maximalist, period-correct projecting marquee.

rules_observations: Vertical stack plus projecting mount is correct for a pedestrian street: the name reads along the sidewalk, not only head-on.
Single dominant element (the stacked name) with the bulb border and faux neon as subordinate framing keeps one primary read.
craft_observations: Three illumination techniques (push-thru white, faux-neon amber, exposed amber lamps) are layered to build a period marquee look while staying all-LED for service life.
Gold/blue/red metallic palette with a bronze center band gives a warm vintage-theater read rather than a flat modern cabinet.

aesthetic_notes.note: The maximalist option: exposed-lamp border plus faux neon plus push-thru is the most animated and most nostalgic of the three.
